text.p: ON THIS DAY 19TH JUNE.
** BIRTHDAYS **
The first Stuart king of England, JAMES I (King JAMES VI of the Scots), was born in 1556.
French mathematician, physician and theologian BLAISE PASCAL, who invented the first calculating machine, was born in 1623.
Explorer HAMILTON HUME, who travelled across much of south-east Australia, was born in Parramatta in 1797. He died in 1873.

Australian cricketer and cricket writer FRANCIS 'NOSS' IREDALE, a renowned slips fielder (his father developed his skills by throwing oranges at him - any that he dropped he couldn't eat), was born in 1867.
American actor CHARLES COBURN, who won an Oscar for "The More The Merrier", was born in 1877.
The DUCHESS OF WINDSOR, WALLIS WARFIELD SIMPSON, the American socialite who lured EDWARD VIII from the English throne, was born in 1896.
School teacher CHRISTOPHER CARROLL, who became Australia's longest-serving teacher (he died in his clasroom in 1975), was born in 1902.
Larger than life Queensland politician RUSS HINZE was born at Oxenford, (situated between Brisbane and the Gold Coast) in 1919.
Comic British singer CHARLIE DRAKE, who had hits with "Splish Splash" (1958) and "My Boomerang Won't Come Back" (1961/62), was born in 1925.

Indian-born author SALMAN AHMED RUSHDIE, who was placed on an Islamic 'hit-list' by Iranian leader AYATOLLAH KHOMEINI following the publication of his controversial book "The Satanic Verses" in 1988, was born in 1947.
American actress KATHLEEN TURNER was born in 1954.
American singer/dancer PAULA ABDUL, whose hits included "(It's Just) The Way That You Love Me" (1988/89) and "Opposites Attract" (1989), was born in 1963.
** EVENTS **
1820 : SIR JOSEPH BANKS, the British botanist who
travelled the world with CAPTAIN JAMES COOK, died at the age of 77.
1829 : British Home Secretary SIR ROBERT PEEL founded the
Metropolitan Police. Officers were dubbed 'Bobbies', in honour of SIR ROBERT.
1846 : The first baseball game with set rules was played
at the Elysian fields in Hoboken New Jersey in the United States.
1885 : The Statue of Liberty arrived in New York, being a
gift from France.
1924 : British climber GEORGE MALLORY disappeared just
300 metres from the summit of Mount Everest, during an attempt to conquer the peak. Whether he reached the peak is one of mountaineering's endurung mysteries.
1931 : Communism supporters and police fought a two hour
street battle the Sydney suburb of Newtown, during the so-called 'Bloody Friday' evictions during the depression.
1937 : The man who created the 'boy who never grew up'
('Peter Pan') Scottish author SIR JAMES MATTHEW BARRIE, died at the age of 77.
1944 : The Battle of the Philippines Sea began when the
Japanese fleet attacked U.S. ships protecting a landing at Saipan This resulted in considerable air and sea losses for Japan.
1953 : 35 year old JULIUS ROSENBERG and his 37 year old
wife ETHEL were sent to the electric chair at Sing Sing in the United States, accused of selling atom bomb secrets to the Soviet Union.
1961 : Evidence was found for the first time proving the
existence of Pontius Pilate when a slab with his name on it was found by an Italian dig at Caesarea in Israel.
1963 : The contraceptive pill was made available to
British women free of charge through the National Health Service.
1967 : The Monterey Pop Festival developed a cult
following, following performances from stars including JIMMY HENDRIX, 'The Who', JANIS JOPLIN, OTIS REDDING and 'The Mamas and the Papas'.
1969 : The Australian Arbitration Commission ruled that
women could be paid at the same rate as men. Much of the campaign for equal pay for women had been fought by the late EDNA RYAN of the Womens' Electoral Lobby.
1977 : British punk group, the 'Sex Pistols', was
attacked for the second day in a row by angry audience members armed with knives. Drummer STEVE COOK was the latest band-member targetted.
1985 : Officials announced that the South Pole had moved

slightly closer to Australia, and was at a point about 144 km from the Antarctic coastline. It was known that the North Pole was stationary but the South Pole drifted continuously, and was plotted every five years or so. 1993 : English novelist Sir WILLIAM GOLDING died at the age
of 81. His first book "Lord Of The Flies" (1954) was about English students turning to savagery after being marooned on a Pacific Island, and he was awarded the Nobel Prize for
Literature in 1983.
1994 : MICHEL ROCARD resigned as head of the French
Socialist party after the movement's national council voted a no-confidence vote against him.
